Surah al-Falaq

Makkan according to al-Hasan, ʿAta', ʿIkrimah, Jabir, and a narration of Kurayb from Ibn ʿAbbas; Madinan according to Ibn ʿAbbas in a narration of Abu Salih, and Qatadah and a group, and this is the sound view, because the occasion of its revelation was the sorcery of the Jews, as will come, God willing, and they only bewitched him, peace and blessings be upon him, in Madinah, as is reported in the Sahih collections. So one should not give heed to whoever affirmed that it is Makkan. The same applies to Surah al-Nas, and its verses are five without any dispute. When the matter of divinity was explained in the surah before it, these two were placed after it as an explanation of what one seeks refuge in God from, namely the evil that is in the ranks of the world and the ranks of its creatures. Both this surah and the one after it were revealed together, as in al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il. For this reason they are paired, along with the fact that they share the name "al-Mu'awwidhatayn" and begin with "Say: I seek refuge."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and others related from him that he said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: "There have been revealed to me tonight verses the like of which I have never seen: Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak, and Say, I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind."
Page 279

al-Bukhari, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah related from ʿAʾisha that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, whenever he went to his bed each night, would join his palms, then blow into them and recite in them: "Say: He is God, One," "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak," and "Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind." Then he would wipe with them as much of his body as he could, beginning with them over his head and face and what faced of his body, doing this three times.

It has come in a hadith that whoever recites them together with Surah al-Ikhlas three times in the evening and three times in the morning, they will suffice him against everything.

There are many reports on their virtue beyond what has been mentioned. And from Ibn Mas'ud, that he denied their Qur'anic status.

Imam Ahmad, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related through sound chains from him that he used to erase the two Mu'awwidhatayn from the mushaf and say: "Do not mix the Qur'an with what is not of it; indeed they are not from the Book of God, the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was only commanded to seek refuge with them." And Ibn Mas'ud would not recite with them. Al-Bazzar said: None of the Companions followed Ibn Mas'ud in this, and it is established from the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, that he recited them in prayer, and they are established in the mushaf.

Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Hibban and others related from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: "I came to Madinah and met Ubayy ibn Ka'b and said to him: O Abu al-Mundhir, I have seen that Ibn Mas'ud does not write the Mu'awwidhatayn in his mushaf. He said: By He who sent Muhammad with the truth, I asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, about them, and no one has asked me about them since I asked, other than you. He said: It was said to me: Say, so I said it. So we say what the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said."

With this disagreement some atheists criticized the inimitability of the Qur'an, saying: If the eloquence of that had reached the level of inimitability, what is not the Qur'an would be distinguished by it, and there would be no disagreement about its being part of it. You know that consensus has been established on the Qur'anic status of the two. They also said: denying that today is disbelief, and perhaps Ibn Mas'ud retracted from that. In Sharh al-Mawaqif it is stated that the disagreement of the Companions about some surahs of the Qur'an is transmitted by single narrators which yield only conjecture, while the collected Qur'an is transmitted by mass transmission which yields certainty, in the face of which conjecture vanishes; so those single reports are not to be heeded. Then, even if we grant their disagreement regarding what has been mentioned, we say: they did not disagree about its being revealed to the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, nor about its reaching the level of inimitability in eloquence, but only about its being part of the Qur'an; and this does no harm to what we are concerned with. End.

The opposite of this view regarding the two surahs mentioned has been said concerning the two surahs of al-Khal' and al-Hafd, whose wording also has variant readings, among them what the Hanafis recite in the qunut. It has been related that they were in the mushaf of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, in the mushaf of Ibn ʿAbbas and in the mushaf of Ibn Mas'ud. So if it is established that they are the speech of God, they are abrogated in recitation and are not from the Qur'an, as is not hidden.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful. "Say: I seek refuge" — i.e., I take refuge, I hold fast, and I guard myself — "in the Lord of the daybreak." Falaq is a form of fa'l in the sense of maf'ul, an adjectival form like qasas in the sense of maqsus, from falaqa: he split and separated. It encompasses all possible existing things, for He split them out from non-existence by the light of origination, especially what emerges from an origin, like springs from mountains, rains from clouds, plants from the earth, and children from wombs. By convention it is restricted to the dawn, and the people's use of "split" for it, together with their saying "God split the night to reveal the dawn," is like the use of "flayed" for a sheep alongside their saying "I stripped the hide from the sheep." Its interpretation in the general sense is reported by Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Ibn ʿAbbas, whose wording is: "al-Falaq" is the creation. al-Tastari reported from him that he interpreted it as the dawn.

He, may God be pleased with him, recited the verse of Zuhayr:

The reliever of distress, whose troops are let down, as the daybreak relieves the gloom of darkness.

This is also reported from Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn Jubayr, al-Qurtubi and Ibn Zayd. On this reading, the seeking of refuge is linked to the Name of the Lord attached to the Falaq, which indicates light after darkness, breadth after constriction, and opening after closure, as a noble promise of granting refuge to the one who seeks it from what he seeks refuge from, and of saving him from it, and a strengthening of his hope by reminding him of some of its parallels, and an added encouragement to him to persevere and to attend to knocking on the door of turning to Him, mighty and majestic. It has been said: in specifying "the Falaq" by mention, it is a model of the Day of Resurrection, for homes are like graves, sleep is the brother of death, and those who leave their homes in the morning, some of them go out to freshness and joy, and some of them go out to demands of debts in distress and evils, toward other conditions which are for the servants most like what will be theirs in the return. In the tafsir of al-Qadi: the word "Lord" here is more fitting than the other names which could be attached to Falaq, according to what has been said, because seeking refuge from harms is a form of nurturing; and on the generalization of Falaq this is evident, as it includes both the one seeking refuge and what he seeks refuge from; and on restricting it to the dawn, it has been said: because it indicates that He, glorified is He, is capable and changes conditions and disturbs states, so He removes worries and troubles. Ibn Sina said, after taking the Falaq to be the darkness of non-existence split by the light of existence: In the mention of the Lord there is a subtle secret from the realities of knowledge: the one who is nurtured does not in any of his states become independent of the Lord, as is seen in the child as long as he is nurtured. Since possible quiddities are not independent of the outpouring of the First Principle, the word "Lord" is mentioned, indeed, to point to that. And in it is another indication from the hidden sciences: seeking refuge and taking refuge in the language are an expression of turning to another. So when he is commanded merely to turn to another, and this is expressed by "Lord," it shows that the non-attainment is not due to a matter returning to the One sought refuge in, the Bestower of good, but to a matter returning to the recipient of it. For it is established that nothing among perfections and others is withheld on the part of the First Principle, glorified is He; rather all is attained, contingent upon the one prepared turning the direction of his receptivity toward it. This is what is meant by the Prophetic indication: "Indeed your Lord has breaths of His mercy during the days of your time; so expose yourselves to them." He showed that the breaths of kindness are constant, and the defect is only from the one prepared. End. In another report from Ibn ʿAbbas, and a group of the Companions and Successors, the Falaq is a pit in Hell.

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami related "from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, who said: I asked the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, about the words of God, mighty and majestic: 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak.' He said: "It is a prison in Hell in which the tyrants and the arrogant are confined, and Hell itself seeks refuge in God from it."

Ibn Mardawayh related "from ʿAmr ibn ʿAnbasa, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, led us in prayer and recited 'Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak,' and said: 'O Ibn ʿAnbasa, do you know what the Falaq is?' I said: God and His Messenger know best. He said: "A well in Hell; when the well is kindled, Hell is kindled from it, so that it is harmed by it just as the son of Adam is harmed by Hell."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ka'b, who said: The Falaq is a house in Hell; when it is opened, the people of the Fire cry out from the intensity of its heat.

From al-Kalbi: it is a valley in Hell. It has also been said: it is Hell itself. According to what is in the Kashshaf, from their saying of what lies low in the earth: falaq, and its plural is fulqan, like khalq and khilqan. As for specifying it by mention, it has been said that it is the dwelling of the Jews. Among the Companions, one of them came to Syria and saw the houses of the People of the Covenant and the ease of life they enjoyed and the worldly abundance granted to them, and said: "I do not care, is there not the Falaq behind them?" It is explained by what was reported above from Ka'b. And among them is the one who bewitched the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, so in linking the seeking of refuge to the Lord attached to it there is a noble promise of granting him, may God bless him and grant him peace, refuge from their evil. It is not hidden that this is not something that satisfies the heart, and I think the earlier reports are weak, and in my view the first meaning of Falaq is preferred.

﴿From the evil of what He created﴾. That is, from the evil of the one He created from the two weighty things (humans and jinn) and others, whatever it may be, of beings endowed with nature and choice. The apparent meaning is that "evil" is general, covering bodily harms and others. Some have claimed that seeking refuge here is only from bodily harms, and that it covers humans and other beings not within the scope of seeking refuge. Then its generality was made the basis for the addition of the Lord to the daybreak (al-Falaq) in the general sense, and that is, as you see, [weak]. Yes, what comes to mind first is that its generality extends to the evils of this world. Some eminent scholars said: it is general to every evil in this world and the Hereafter, the evil of humans, jinn and devils, the evil of predatory beasts and venomous creatures, the evil of the Fire, the evil of sins, of desire, the evil of the self, and the evil of deeds. Its apparent sense is the generalization of "what He created" such that it includes the very self of the one seeking refuge. Nothing prevents this from the revelation of the sura so that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) might seek refuge with it. Some have permitted making "mā" a verbal particle (mā maṣdariyyah) with the verbal noun interpreted as a passive participle, but that is an unnecessary strain. The attribution of evil to "what He created" was said to be because it is specific to the world of creation, founded on the mixing of differing substances, which entails generation and corruption. As for the world of command (ʿĀlam al-Amr), which came into being by the mere word "Be" without material, it is pure good, entirely free from any admixture of evil. The apparent meaning is that by the world of command he meant the world of the immaterial beings, namely the angels, peace be upon them. It was objected, setting aside the fact that this does not appear in the language of the Sharia, that among them there are those from whom evil proceeds, such as the sinking of lands and the punishment of servants. It was answered that this is by His command, so it proceeds only in executing the command, not for the purpose of evil as such, so there is no objection. Yes, it is objected that their being immaterial contradicts the preferred view held by the early community (al-Salaf) and those who followed them; rather, they are subtle luminous bodies. And even if their immateriality is granted, we say that the immaterial beings are not confined to them. How so, when many have held that the jinn are immaterial, saying: they are not bodies nor inhering in bodies, but are immaterial substances subsisting by themselves, differing in quiddity, some of them good, some of them evil, some noble, free, loving of goodness, and some base, vile, loving of evils and calamities. In sum, "what He created" is more general than the immaterial, according to the view that they are such, and than others; and all of it is created by Him, Exalted, that is, brought into existence by choice after non-existence. Except that what is meant is seeking refuge from whatever in it is evil.

Ibn Fa'id (ʿAmr ibn Fāʾid), as reported in al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), read "min sharrin" with tanwin. Ibn ʿAṭiyyah said: this is the reading of ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd and some of the Mu'tazilah (the Mu'tazilah, a rationalist theological school), who hold that Allah, Exalted, did not create evil. They took "mā" as negation and made the clause in the position of a qualifier; that is, "from the evil of what Allah, Exalted, did not create and did not bring into being." He said: this is a rejected reading, based on a false doctrine, end of quote. You know that the reading is by transmission, and this interpretation is not necessarily fixed for this reading; rather, "mā" may be a substitute (badal) for "sharr" with an elided word, omitted because of what precedes it, meaning: from the evil of the evil of what He created.

﴿And from the evil of the darkening night﴾ — the singling out of some evils for mention, although they are included in what precedes, is to increase the sense of need to seek refuge from them, because of how frequently they occur. Also, specifying what one seeks refuge from is more indicative of earnestness in seeking refuge and more likely to bring protection. The ghasiq (الغاسِق, the darkening one) is the night when its darkness intensifies. The root meaning of ghasaq is fullness; it is said: "ghasaqat al-ʿayn" when the eye became full of tears. It was also said that it means flowing, and ghasaq al-layl (the darkness of night) is the pouring down of its darkness, used metaphorically; ghasaq al-ʿayn is the flowing of its tears. The attribution of evil to the night is because it is associated with it, since it occurs in it, in the manner of the saying: "its day is fasting." Its being indefinite (شَرِّ) is for the generality of evil's inclusion of all its individual instances and all its parts.

﴿When it comes to cover﴾ — that is, when its darkness enters into everything. The root meaning of waqb is a hollow and a pit, and then it was used for entering. From it is the saying of the poet:

"The punishment encompassed them, so it was as if the hot wind's fire had reached them, and they were extinguished."

Likewise, it is used for setting (al-maghib), since that is like entering into a waqb, i.e., a hollow and a pit. It has also been explained here as "coming." The restriction to this time is because the occurrence of evil in it is more frequent, and guarding against it is more difficult and arduous. Among their proverbs: "The night is more concealing for the calamity." The explanation of ghasiq as the night and waqb as the entering of its darkness was transmitted by Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir from Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, and Ibn Abi Hatim from al-Dahhak. It was also narrated from al-Hasan, and al-Zajjaj adopted it, except that he took ghasiq to mean "cold," and said: it was applied to the night because it is colder than the day.

Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it is the day, and "waqaba" means "entered into the night," and this, as you see, is far-fetched. It was also said: it is the moon when it is full of light, given that ghasaq means fullness, and its waqb is its entering into eclipse and its darkening. It was also said: it is called ghasiq because of the swiftness of its movement and its crossing of the mansions (zodiacal lodges), given that ghasaq is metaphorically from flowing. It was also said: it is so named because its body is dark and it only gains light from the sun's light, and its waqb, according to both opinions, is the dark phase (al-mihaq) at the end of the month. The astrologers count it as an inauspicious time, and for this reason sorcerers do not undertake sorcery that causes illness except at that time. It was said: this is the one suited to the occasion of revelation, and its explanation as the moon has been supported by what al-Imam Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others transmitted: "From ʿAʾisha, she said: One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the moon when it rose, and said: 'O ʿAʾisha, seek refuge with Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it comes to cover.'"

Whoever accepts the authenticity of this should not turn to another explanation.

Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn Shihab that he said: the ghasiq is the sun when it sets, and perhaps its being called ghasiq is because it is full of light. Ibn Zayd reported from the Arabs that the ghasiq is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), and its waqb is its setting, and diseases and plagues would increase at that time. Many narrators transmitted this explanation from Abu Hurayrah as a marfu' report.

And in a hadith: "When the star rises, the blight is lifted."

In some narrations there is an addition: "from the Arabian Peninsula."

In some of them: "Never does the star rise on a morning but that every calamity or blight is lifted or lessened."

There are other narrations on this; let the Great Commentary of al-Manawi on al-Jami' al-Saghir be consulted. It was also said that it refers to the snake when it bites, and its being called ghasiq is because it is full of poison and death; what is meant is its poison when it enters the body, and it was called ghasiq because of its flowing from its fang. Neither of these two opinions is to be relied upon. It was also said: it is every evil that befalls a person, and evil is described with darkness and blackness, and its waqb is its onset. Al-Majd al-Fayruzabadi in al-Qamus, under the root w-q-b, mentioned an opinion on the meaning of the verse which he claimed al-Ghazali and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas; I do not think its attribution to him is sound, since it is evidently a weak opinion among the views.

[Page 283]

﴿And from the evil of those who blow upon knots﴾: that is, from the evil of the female sorceresses who tie knots in threads and blow upon them. So "those who blow" (al-naffathat) is a description of the souls (al-nufus), and the feminine form was used in consideration of the feminine noun. The influence of magic comes only from evil souls and wicked spirits, and its power derives from them. Some scholars supposed that the word described (mawsuf) is "women," but the first view is preferable, because it includes men, encompasses the earlier allusion, and fits the occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul). The one who bewitched the Prophet (ﷺ) was, according to the well-known report, a man, as you will hear, God willing.

It was said: some women helped him. Because such practices are typically women's work and their guile, the feminine form predominates over the masculine here. This is permissible, as al-Khafaji explained in his commentary on Durrat al-Ghawwas. Al-nafth (blowing) means blowing with saliva, as al-Zamakhshari said. The author of al-Lawami' said: it is like blowing, which occurs in incantation (ruqyah) without saliva; if saliva is emitted, it is spitting (tafl). The first view is more correct, because of what Ibn al-Qayyim reported: when they practise sorcery and seek to make their act effective, they use a breath mixed with some part of their wicked souls.

al-Hasan read "al-nuffathat" with a damma on the nun. He, Ibn 'Umar, 'Abdullah ibn al-Qasim and Ya'qub (in one transmission) read "al-nafithat," and Abu al-Rabi' and al-Hasan also read "al-nafithat" without an alif, like "al-hadhirat." Their definiteness (al-ta'rif) is either for a known reference (al-'ahd) or to announce that the evil encompasses all of them and that they are wholly devoted to it. Its mention specifically is due to what al-Bukhari, Muslim and Ibn Majah related from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was bewitched, to the extent that he imagined he had done something when he had not done it. Then one day, or one night, he prayed to Allah, then prayed, then prayed again, and then said: 'Are you aware, O 'A'ishah, that Allah has given me a ruling on what I asked Him about?' I said: 'What is it, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'Two men came to me; one sat at my head and the other at my feet. The one at my head said to the one at my feet, or the one at my feet to the one at my head: "What is the ailment of this man?" He said: "He is bewitched (matbub)." He asked: "Who bewitched him?" He said: "Labid ibn al-A'sam." He asked: "With what?" He said: "With a comb, the hair from a comb, and the dried spathe of a male palm." He asked: "Where is it?" He said: "In the well of Dhi Arwan."'"

She said: "Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to it with some of his companions, then said: 'O 'A'ishah, by Allah, its water is as if it were the infusion of henna, and its palm trees are as if they were the heads of devils.' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, would you not burn it?' He said: 'No. As for me, Allah has granted me well-being, and I disliked stirring up evil among people.' Then he ordered it to be buried."

These two angels, according to what is indicated by the report of Ibn Mardawayh through 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas, were Jibril and Mika'il, upon them be peace. From their narration in al-Bayhaqi's Dala'il, after mentioning the hadith of the two angels: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arose the next morning with his companions, he went to the well, and a man entered and extracted the dried spathe from beneath the rawu'ah (the stone at the mouth of the well). In it was the comb of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and some of the hair from his head, and there was a figure of wax resembling the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and in it were pins stuck in, and there was a string with eleven knots. Then Jibril, upon him be peace, came to him with the two Mu'awwidhatayn and said: 'O Muhammad, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾,' and a knot was undone; '﴿from the evil of what He has created﴾,' and a knot was undone, until he finished both surahs and undid all the knots. Whenever he removed one, he felt pain from it, and then he would find relief after that." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, would you not kill the Jew?" He said: "Allah has granted me well-being, and what he sees of the punishment of Allah is worse."

In another report: "The one who undertook the sorcery was Labid ibn al-A'sam and his daughters. The Prophet (ﷺ) fell ill, so Jibril descended with the Mu'awwidhatayn and informed him of the location of the magic, of who had worked it and with what. The Prophet (ﷺ) then sent 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, al-Zubayr and 'Ammar, and they emptied the water of the well, which was like the infusion of henna. Then they lifted the rawu'ah of the well and brought out the teeth of the comb, and with them a string in which eleven knots had been tied and pierced with pins. They brought them to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he began to recite the Mu'awwidhatayn over them. Whenever he recited a verse, a knot came undone, and he (upon him be prayers and peace) found lightness, until the last knot was undone at the completion of the two surahs." Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "It is as if he had been released from a tether..." and the report continues.

The first report is more sound than this one.

Imam al-Mazari said: Innovators (al-mubtadi'ah) have denied this hadith on the grounds that it lowers the rank of prophethood and casts doubt upon it, and that accepting it prevents trust in the Shari'ah. It was answered that the hadith is sound, and it does not contradict the text nor entail a lowering of the rank of prophethood or doubt about it. The disbelievers, by their saying "bewitched," meant that he was mad, and far be that from him. And even if the apparent meaning is intended, it would have been before this incident. Or what they meant is that magic had an effect on him and that what came to him of revelation was imaginings of magic, which is also false, because Allah protected him in what relates to the message. As for matters of worldly affairs for which he was not sent, and which are among the things that befall human beings, it is not far-fetched that he would imagine things that have no reality. It has been said: he imagined that he had had intercourse with his wives when he had not, and a person may imagine such a thing in a dream, so it is not unlikely that he imagines it while awake. It was also said: he imagined that he had done something when he had not done it, but he did not believe the correctness of what he imagined, so his beliefs (upon him be prayers and peace) remained sound.

Qadi 'Iyad said: The reports of the hadith of 'A'ishah have come explaining that magic only had power over his noble body (ﷺ) and the outward limbs, not over his intellect, his heart, or his conviction (upon him be prayers and peace). The meaning of what is in some reports, "until he thought he had come to his wives and had not come to them," and in some, "he imagined that..." etc.: that there appeared to him from his vigour and his customary ability over them, but when he approached them, the seizure of magic gripped him, so he did not come to them and was unable to do so, as happens to the one who is bewitched. Whatever is in the reports, that he (upon him be prayers and peace) imagined doing something and had not done it, or similar, is to be understood as imagination through sight, not a defect that entered his intellect. There is nothing in that which introduces confusion regarding the message, nor provides a basis for the people of error (ahl al-dalalah) to criticize. End of quotation.

Some scholars denied the very existence of magic and negated its reality, attributing what occurs from it to false imaginings with no realities. The doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah and the scholars of the community is to affirm it, and that it has a reality like the reality of other things, because of the evidence of the Book and the Sunnah for this. And it is not deemed unreasonable by the intellect that Allah breaks the customary order when a composite speech is uttered, or when specific bodies are composed, or when powers are combined in an arrangement known only to the sorcerer. When a person observes that some substances are deadly, like poisons, some cause sickness, like harsh medicines, and some are harmful, like medicines that counter a disease, his intellect does not find it strange that a sorcerer might be alone in knowing deadly powers, or a destructive speech, or something that leads to separation.

[Page 284]

Yet it does not lack a psychological effect. Then, those who affirm it differed about the extent of its effect. Some said: its effect does not exceed the extent of separation between a man and his wife, because Allah mentioned that only to magnify what occurs through it and to inspire awe of it; had it an effect greater than that, He would have mentioned it, since an example is not struck in exaggeration except with the highest state of what is mentioned. The doctrine of the Ash'ariyyah is that it is possible for it to have an effect greater than that, and this is the rational correct view, because there is no agent except Allah, and whatever occurs of that is a custom that Allah has established. The acts do not differ in this, and none of them is more deserving than another. The Shari'ah's report that its effect is limited to a certain level would necessitate adopting that, but there is no decisive text requiring restriction to what the first speaker said. The mention of separation between the spouses in the verse is not an explicit text prohibiting an increase; the only question is whether it is apparent or not. The distinction between the sorcerer and the prophet or the saint (wali), according to the Ash'ariyyah who hold that breaking customary order may occur at the hand of a sorcerer, is explained in the theological books and other commentaries on the Sahih collections.

It was said regarding the verse: the meaning of blowing on knots is nullifying men's resolutions through stratagems, borrowed from softening knots by blowing saliva on them so that they may be easily undone. This is close to the innovated interpretations (bida' al-tafasir).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 113, verse 5:**

﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾. That is: when he manifests what is in his soul of envy and acts upon its requirement, by arranging the preliminaries of evil and the beginnings of harm against the envied person, in word and in deed. Among this, according to what has been said, is looking at the envied person and directing his wicked soul toward him in a manner of anger; for the soul of the envier at that time takes on a wicked disposition, which may affect the envied person, according to his weakness and the strength of the envier's soul, with an evil that may reach the point of destruction. And many an envier harms by his look, with the eye of his envy, in the manner in which some snakes harm by their gaze.

They mentioned that the one who causes harm by the evil eye (al-ʿa'in) and the envier share in that each of them takes on a disposition of soul and is directed toward the one whom he wishes to harm, except that the one who causes harm by the evil eye takes on this disposition at the moment of facing and beholding, while the envier's envy occurs both in the absence and in the presence. Also, the one who causes harm by the evil eye may harm an animal or crop that he does not envy, although he is never free of the envy of its owner. The restriction by this is because there is no harm (in the absence of envy); rather it has been said that the harm of envy only falls upon the envier and no one else, as ʿAli, may God ennoble his face, said: "How excellent is envy in its justice! It begins with its possessor and kills him."

And Ibn al-Muʿtazz said:

Be patient with the envy of the envious, for your patience is its killer.
The fire devours its own part, if it finds nothing else to devour.

It should be known that envy (al-hasad) is applied to wishing for the removal of another's blessing, and to wishing that the absence of blessing and the continuation of the other's deficiency or poverty or the like remain. The first application is the most common. The envier, under both applications, is detested by God Most High and by His servants, ʿAzza wa Jall, and commits a major sin according to what is well known among them. But the verified view is that natural, innate envy, if its possessor does not act upon its requirement of harm in any way, but rather treats his brother with what God Most High loves, striving against his own soul, is not sinful; rather its possessor is rewarded for his striving against his soul and his good treatment of his brother with a great reward, because of the hardship of opposing one's natural disposition, as is not hidden. Envy is also applied, metaphorically, to ghibta (desire for a similar blessing), and this was common in the first usage. It is wishing that one would have a like blessing to that of his brother, without wishing its removal, and this is not objectionable. Among this is what is authentically reported from the saying of the Messenger of God, may God's blessings and peace be upon him: "There is no envy except in two: a man whom God has given wealth and empowered him to spend it in the right way, and a man whom God has given wisdom, so he judges by it and teaches it to the people."

And Abu Tammam said:

They envied him, but they are not to be blamed for his glory,
and no envier among the noble deeds is (truly) an envier.

And he also said:

Excuse your envious one regarding what you have been singled out for,
for exaltedness is fine, and envy is apt in its like.

Furthermore, Ibn Sina said: the "darkness when it grows dark" (al-ghasiq) is the animal faculty, which is a dark, gloomy obscurity, contrary to the rational soul, which is the one seeking refuge. For it was created in its essence pure, clear, free of the turbidities of matter and its attachments, receptive to all forms and realities; it is only tainted by the animal faculty. The "blowers in the knots" (al-naffathat fi al-ʿuqad) are an allusion to the vegetative faculties,
Page 285
in that they increase the magnitude in all its directions, length, breadth and depth; so it is as if they blow into the three knots. And since the connection between the human soul and the vegetative faculties is through the animal faculty, he has indeed mentioned the animal faculties before the vegetative faculties. The evil necessarily resulting from these two faculties in the essence of the soul is the firm establishment of the bodily attachments and the prevention of its nourishment by the food suitable to it and fitting to its essence, which is the encompassing of the kingdom of the heavens and the earth and the imprinting with the lasting impressions. By His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾ he intended the conflict arising between the body and its faculties and the soul; so the envier is the body insofar as it possesses the two faculties, and the envied is the soul; thus the body is a burden upon it. How good is its state when it turns away from it, and how great is its delight in separation, if it has not been tainted by it.

It has also been said: "the darkness" refers to the mineral, "the blowers" to plants, and "the envier" to animals. And since man is not harmed by the celestial bodies but is harmed by elemental bodies, which are either mineral, plant or animal, he was commanded to seek refuge from the evil of each of them. Both views, as you see, are (weak). And God Most High knows best.
